lessons.title: Personal data and identifiability
lessons.objective: Distinguish personal, pseudonymized and anonymous information.
concepts: Personal data concern an identified or identifiable natural person. Identification can be indirect; a name is not required.
Pseudonymization separates identifying information from the remaining data. It reduces risk but does not automatically make data anonymous.
Anonymity requires considering means reasonably likely to be used to identify a person, taking account of context and available technology.
lessons.example: A student research assistant replaces interviewees’ names with codes and keeps the key separately. The coded records still relate to identifiable participants.
lessons.nuance: Identifiability is contextual. Removing direct identifiers does not establish that a dataset is anonymous; consider linkage and small groups.

questions.statement: A student number can be personal data even when a name is absent.
questions.explanation: An identifier can enable indirect identification.

questions.statement: Keeping a code key in a separate secure location makes the coded records anonymous for the university.
questions.explanation: The university can still link records to individuals; separation is a safeguard.

questions.statement: A group-level statistic can fall outside GDPR if no natural person is reasonably identifiable.
questions.explanation: Genuinely anonymous information is outside GDPR’s personal-data scope.

lessons.title: Overview: principles and lawful bases
lessons.objective: Identify a purpose and lawful basis before processing.
concepts: Article 5 sets principles including fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, security and accountability.
Article 6 requires an applicable lawful basis. Public task must have a basis in EU or member-state law; consent is not a universal default.
Special-category data require an applicable Article 9 condition in addition to Article 6.

**How to study this topic.** The following eleven lessons separate the individual principles and lawful bases. In practice, start with a defined purpose, identify an applicable basis, check all Article 5 principles, then assess additional conditions (including Article 9, if relevant). These tests are cumulative, not alternatives.

**Legal hierarchy.** Read the operative articles first, then the associated recitals for context. Regulatory guidance and judgments assist interpretation; a local university rule can establish a process or retention schedule but cannot override binding law.
lessons.example: A university collects only details necessary to administer enrollment under its relevant legal duties.
lessons.nuance: A university cannot assume that every activity is a public task. Identify the actual purpose and legal basis; Article 6(1)(f) is unavailable to public authorities when performing their tasks.

questions.statement: A lawful basis makes the data-minimization principle optional.
questions.explanation: The principles apply alongside the lawful basis.

questions.statement: A public-task basis needs a foundation in EU or member-state law.
questions.explanation: Article 6(3) requires the legal basis for processing under Article 6(1)(e).

questions.statement: An Article 9 condition replaces the need for an Article 6 lawful basis.
questions.explanation: Both layers must be addressed for special-category processing.

lessons.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
lessons.objective: Explain why having a legal basis does not by itself make processing fair or transparent.
concepts: **Three distinct tests.** Lawfulness asks whether the processing has a valid basis and satisfies applicable legal conditions. Fairness asks whether the way people are treated is justified, including their reasonable expectations and the consequences for them. Transparency asks whether individuals can understand the processing. Meeting one test does not automatically meet the others.

**Read the law.** Start with Article 5(1)(a), then Articles 12–14. Article 12 concerns understandable and accessible communication. Article 13 applies to collection from the individual, while Article 14 addresses other sources, subject to its own exceptions and timing.

**Information is not consent.** A privacy notice explains what happens; it is not itself a lawful basis. If the university relies on a legal obligation, asking a student to accept a notice does not change the legal basis. If it relies on consent, the separate Article 7 requirements must be met.

**Fairness in practice.** A system may technically comply with a stated purpose but still disadvantage a group through inaccurate inputs or unexpected use. Examine the actual consequences, available alternatives and whether the person could reasonably anticipate the processing.
lessons.example: A course platform collects activity logs for technical support. The university wants to use them to identify supposedly disengaged students and send alerts to teachers. A general privacy notice about platform administration does not by itself resolve the new purpose, lawful basis, proportionality or risk of incorrect inferences. Compare a voluntary support service with a system that affects assessment.
lessons.nuance: Transparency does not require publishing other people's personal data or confidential technical details indiscriminately. Article 14 exceptions must be assessed rather than assumed; a difficult notification process alone does not create an exemption.

questions.statement: A clear privacy notice establishes a lawful basis by itself.
questions.explanation: A notice fulfills information duties; the legal basis is a separate Article 6 question.

questions.statement: A university relying on legal obligation still has transparency duties.
questions.explanation: Article 13 generally applies even where consent is not the basis.

questions.statement: A technically accurate student profile may still be unfair in its intended use.
questions.explanation: Accuracy is distinct from fairness; consequences and context matter.

questions.statement: Article 14 is relevant when data are obtained from another institution rather than the student.
questions.explanation: Indirect collection brings Article 14 into consideration, including its exceptions.

questions.statement: Making a processing activity clear to students removes the need to examine necessity.
questions.explanation: Transparency does not displace minimization or the requirements of the chosen basis.

questions.statement: A student must consent to a privacy notice for processing based on a statutory obligation to be lawful.
questions.explanation: Consent is not required as an additional legal basis when Article 6(1)(c) validly applies.

lessons.title: Purpose limitation and further processing
lessons.objective: Distinguish a purpose from a method, and evaluate whether a new use is compatible.
concepts: **Start with the objective.** A purpose is the reason for processing, not the software, the data format or the department involved. A vague label such as improving education is not enough to explain why particular data are needed. Write a purpose at a level that permits a meaningful necessity assessment.

**A new use is a separate question.** Article 6(4) identifies compatibility factors when further processing is not based on consent or qualifying EU or national law: the relationship between purposes, the collection context, the nature of the data, consequences and safeguards. Recital 50 explains the rationale. Compatible processing does not automatically need a separate basis from the original one, but the original basis must actually support the continued processing.

**Research is special, not unrestricted.** Article 5(1)(b) treats further processing for scientific research as compatible subject to Article 89(1). The research purpose must be genuine and safeguards appropriate. The research rule does not erase Article 9 conditions, transparency duties or legal restrictions.

**Document a change.** Identify the proposed new objective, what data it needs, who gets access, what individuals were told and what consequences are possible. Where required, inform individuals before processing for a new purpose.
lessons.example: A university collected exam marks to determine whether students passed. A team wants to study whether teaching methods affect outcomes. Compare research using coded marks with an operational dashboard that predicts which individual students should be excluded from a course. The two proposed uses have different purposes, consequences and safeguards.
lessons.nuance: Article 6(4) is not itself a seventh lawful basis. Where the proposed use is outside what the original consent covers, do not treat a compatibility analysis as a way to bypass consent restrictions.

questions.statement: The name of a software platform is sufficient to specify the purpose of processing.
questions.explanation: A purpose describes why processing occurs, not merely the tool used.

questions.statement: The nature of the data is relevant to the Article 6(4) compatibility analysis.
questions.explanation: The factors expressly include sensitive and criminal-offence data.

questions.statement: The research compatibility rule depends on Article 89 safeguards.
questions.explanation: The research provision explicitly refers to Article 89(1).

questions.statement: Article 6(4) is an independent lawful basis equivalent to consent.
questions.explanation: The six bases are in Article 6(1); paragraph 4 addresses further-use compatibility.

questions.statement: A compatible new purpose can still trigger a duty to give information about the new use.
questions.explanation: Articles 13(3) and 14(4) require further-purpose information in applicable cases.

questions.statement: Access controls alone resolve all questions about whether a new purpose is compatible.
questions.explanation: Safeguards are only one of several relevant factors.

lessons.title: Data minimization and proportionality
lessons.objective: Evaluate the necessity of data fields, granularity, access and collection methods.
concepts: **Minimize relative to purpose.** Article 5(1)(c) requires an appropriate relationship between the data collected and the specified purpose. The smallest possible dataset is not always sufficient; the correct question is whether each element is justified. Inadequate data can also lead to unreliable decisions.

**Consider alternatives.** Compare full dates of birth with age bands, recorded interviews with notes, continuous monitoring with targeted checks and raw records with statistics. Ask whether a less intrusive approach would achieve the same objective effectively. Cost or convenience alone is not a blanket justification.

**Minimization extends beyond fields.** Article 25(2) addresses the amount collected, extent of processing, storage and accessibility. Restrict access by role and purpose. A legitimate need for one staff member does not justify access by an entire faculty.

**Research design matters.** Scientific validity may require granular variables or longitudinal linkage. Justify such choices based on the research question and methodology, then limit unnecessary identifiers, separate linkage keys and consider later aggregation.
lessons.example: A study needs to compare performance across age groups. The team requests exact dates of birth, addresses and full student names. If only age bands and a study identifier are needed, those alternatives should be considered. A second study may genuinely need exact age at each measurement; that different purpose could justify greater precision.
lessons.nuance: Minimization does not mean deliberately collecting inadequate information or destroying records that must be retained. It requires a defensible link between the specific purpose and the amount, precision and accessibility of data.

questions.statement: Access limited to staff who need identifiable records is relevant to data protection by default.
questions.explanation: Article 25(2) expressly covers accessibility.

questions.statement: Collecting a field because it may be useful for an unspecified future project satisfies minimization.
questions.explanation: The need must relate to a defined purpose, not speculative future use.

questions.statement: A study can justify exact age rather than age bands if scientific validity requires it.
questions.explanation: Necessity depends on the specified objective and alternatives.

questions.statement: Encrypting a dataset automatically makes every variable in it necessary.
questions.explanation: Security and minimization address different requirements.

questions.statement: A DPIA includes an assessment of necessity and proportionality.
questions.explanation: This is an express part of the DPIA content.

questions.statement: A controller can disregard minimization when processing under a legal obligation.
questions.explanation: The principles continue to apply regardless of the Article 6 basis.

lessons.title: Accuracy and storage limitation
lessons.objective: Distinguish accurate historical evidence from inaccurate current data and justify retention schedules.
concepts: **Accuracy depends on purpose.** Correct an inaccurate current address used to send official correspondence. A historical address in a record of what was reported at an earlier time may be accurate as a historical fact. Record corrections and context rather than silently rewriting evidence.

**Reasonable steps.** The controller must take reasonable measures to correct or erase inaccurate data relevant to the purpose. Consider who entered a value, how it is checked, how the person can challenge it and whether downstream recipients need to be informed.

**Retention is purpose-specific.** Identify when the purpose ends, relevant statutory or contractual constraints, review dates and disposal methods. Different parts of a student file or research project may need different retention periods. GDPR does not create a general ten-year rule.

**Longer research storage.** Article 5(1)(e) allows extended retention when processing is solely for specified archiving, research or statistical purposes, subject to Article 89 safeguards. This is not a general permission to retain all operational data indefinitely.
lessons.example: An exam board retains the formal result and decision record while an assessment platform also stores webcam recordings and working notes. Compare the necessity and legal retention basis of each category. A decision record may need to be preserved while intrusive monitoring data may not.
lessons.nuance: Rectification does not necessarily mean deleting a disputed professional opinion; distinguish accurate recording of an opinion from inaccurate underlying facts, and consider adding a supplementary statement under Article 16.

questions.statement: A historical record can remain accurate even when the person's current circumstances have changed.
questions.explanation: Accuracy is judged in relation to the purpose of the record.

questions.statement: GDPR gives all university records a uniform retention period.
questions.explanation: Retention must be justified by purpose and applicable rules.

questions.statement: Extended research storage is subject to Article 89 safeguards.
questions.explanation: The storage principle expressly conditions longer research retention on safeguards.

questions.statement: The right to rectification requires overwriting every disputed historical record.
questions.explanation: The distinction between inaccurate facts and a faithful historical record matters; supplementary statements can be relevant.

questions.statement: A retention requirement for final grades automatically applies to every recording used in producing the grades.
questions.explanation: Each data category needs its own retention justification.

questions.statement: Accuracy obligations apply to inferred information used to make decisions.
questions.explanation: Personal data used in decision-making must be accurate in relation to their purpose.

lessons.title: Integrity, confidentiality and risk-based security
lessons.objective: Understand the relationship between the security principle and Article 32 measures.
concepts: **Three security dimensions.** Confidentiality concerns unauthorized disclosure or access; integrity concerns unauthorized or accidental alteration; availability concerns loss of access. Security is broader than preventing hackers from reading data.

**Risk-based measures.** Article 32 requires measures suited to the risks, considering technical possibilities, implementation costs, processing context and risks to individuals. Encryption, access restrictions, resilient backups and periodic testing are examples, not an identical mandatory checklist for every activity.

**Institutional context.** A research dataset containing health observations may require more stringent access management than a public event registration list. Evaluate both the likelihood and severity of harm, including re-identification and inappropriate sharing.

**Verify controls.** A policy or supplier promise is not proof that a safeguard works. Consider permission reviews, restoration tests, incident reporting, secure deletion and whether staff know how to use the system safely.
lessons.example: A thesis dataset is accidentally deleted. A backup exists but cannot be restored, and the original files are unavailable. This is an availability problem and may constitute a personal data breach even if no unauthorized person received a copy. Assess separately whether authority notification and individual communication are required.
lessons.nuance: Encryption is valuable but not synonymous with anonymity. Lost encrypted devices may present lower confidentiality risk, but other dimensions and the actual accessibility of the data must still be examined.

questions.statement: Loss of access to personal data can qualify as a personal data breach.
questions.explanation: The breach definition includes accidental or unlawful loss or destruction.

questions.statement: Article 32 requires the same security controls for every processing activity.
questions.explanation: Appropriate controls depend on context and risk.

questions.statement: Testing whether backups can actually be restored is relevant to Article 32.
questions.explanation: Resilience, restoration and testing are expressly relevant.

questions.statement: An encrypted data file is necessarily anonymous.
questions.explanation: Encryption does not automatically prevent reasonable identification.

questions.statement: Security measures can include organizational procedures as well as technical controls.
questions.explanation: Article 32 refers to both technical and organizational measures.

questions.statement: A supplier's security certificate removes the need for the university to assess its processing risks.
questions.explanation: The controller retains risk-based responsibilities.

lessons.title: Accountability and demonstrability
lessons.objective: Explain how a controller demonstrates compliance without confusing paperwork with actual safeguards.
concepts: **Accountability has two components.** The controller must comply with the Article 5 principles and be able to demonstrate that compliance. A signed form is not enough if actual access, retention or data use contradicts it.

**Evidence follows the risk.** A routine administrative process may be documented through a processing record, lawful-basis reasoning and established controls. Higher-risk monitoring may need a DPIA, a decision on alternatives, stronger controls and periodic review. Avoid paperwork that duplicates an existing valid assessment.

**Roles differ.** The controller is responsible for compliance. The DPO provides independent advice and monitoring; the processor implements its own applicable obligations and follows instructions. A university can allocate operational tasks internally without transferring its legal accountability to a coordinator.

**Accountability is ongoing.** New purposes, new recipients, changed software, access from another country or substantially changed risks can require reassessment. Keep decisions and safeguards current rather than treating approval as permanent.
lessons.example: A university introduced a course platform several years ago. A vendor adds an AI feature that uses student interactions for analytics. An old DPA and an old risk assessment may still be useful, but they must be compared with the new functionality. The process owner should identify changes and involve the appropriate specialists.
lessons.nuance: An Article 30 record describes processing; a DPIA assesses high risks. Neither document replaces the other when both are required. The DPO must be involved appropriately and independently, not made responsible for approving their own monitored decisions.

questions.statement: The controller must be able to demonstrate compliance with Article 5 principles.
questions.explanation: This is the accountability requirement in Article 5(2).

questions.statement: A completed processing register proves that every recorded processing operation is lawful.
questions.explanation: A register documents processing but does not establish substantive compliance by itself.

questions.statement: A significant change in processing risks can require review of a prior DPIA.
questions.explanation: Article 35(11) calls for review when risk changes, where necessary.

questions.statement: Assigning privacy tasks to an employee transfers the university's controller accountability to that employee.
questions.explanation: Internal allocation does not change controller responsibility.

questions.statement: An independent DPO advises and monitors rather than taking over controller accountability.
questions.explanation: Articles 38 and 39 describe independence and tasks.

questions.statement: Every accountability requirement can be satisfied by signing a DPA.
questions.explanation: A processor agreement covers only part of the controller's wider obligations.

lessons.title: The six lawful bases
lessons.objective: Compare all Article 6 bases and distinguish necessity from convenience.
concepts: **Consent (a).** A genuine choice for a specified purpose; Article 7 sets additional conditions. It may be suitable for an optional activity, not necessarily for unavoidable student or employee administration.

**Contract (b).** Processing necessary to perform a contract with the individual, or take requested pre-contract steps. Merely including a processing activity in contract terms does not make it necessary.

**Legal obligation (c) and public task (e).** Both need a basis in EU or member-state law under Article 6(3). A specific legal duty is different from processing necessary for a legally grounded public-interest task. Identify the actual relevant duty or task.

**Vital interests (d).** Protects vital interests of an individual, typically urgent or serious situations. It is not a general basis for institutional safety administration. Recital 46 explains that another basis may be preferable when available.

**Legitimate interests (f).** Requires a legitimate interest, necessity and balancing against individual interests and rights. Public authorities cannot rely on it when performing their tasks. Article 9 conditions are additional where special categories are processed.
lessons.example: Compare a student grade record required by law, an optional alumni newsletter, a requested service contract and disclosure of essential information during a medical emergency. The four activities have different purposes and possible legal bases. Determine the actual conditions rather than assigning one basis to the entire university.
lessons.nuance: A controller must determine and communicate the appropriate basis before processing. Do not select multiple speculative bases merely as fallbacks. Different processing operations can legitimately have different bases.

questions.statement: Processing necessary for a contract with the individual may qualify under Article 6(1)(b).
questions.explanation: The contractual basis covers necessary performance or requested pre-contract steps.

questions.statement: A vendor contract between two institutions makes student monitoring necessary under Article 6(1)(b).
questions.explanation: That basis concerns a contract with the data subject or requested steps, and necessity still matters.

questions.statement: Vital interests is a distinct lawful basis from public task.
questions.explanation: They are separately listed in Article 6(1)(d) and (e).

questions.statement: A general institutional policy creates a statutory legal obligation under Article 6(1)(c).
questions.explanation: The basis must be grounded in applicable EU or member-state law.

questions.statement: Article 9 may require an additional condition even if Article 6 is satisfied.
questions.explanation: Special-category processing is subject to a separate prohibition and exceptions.

questions.statement: A public authority performing its public task can rely on Article 6(1)(f) whenever the task is convenient.
questions.explanation: The final sentence of Article 6(1) excludes that use by public authorities.

lessons.title: Consent and power imbalance
lessons.objective: Recognize valid consent, granular choice, withdrawal and the difference from participation consent.
concepts: **Four characteristics.** Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Silence, inactivity or a preselected option does not establish affirmative consent. Explicit consent under Article 9(2)(a) requires a heightened expression.

**Freedom and dependency.** Students may fear academic consequences and employees may fear disadvantage. Recital 43 highlights power imbalances. A university must assess whether refusal or withdrawal can occur without detriment; consent is not categorically impossible in every university relationship.

**Separate purposes.** A student may agree to appear in an optional promotional video but decline later marketing use. Choices should reflect distinct purposes when appropriate; bundling unrelated purposes can undermine freedom and specificity.

**Withdrawal.** Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. It affects future consent-based processing, not the lawfulness of processing before withdrawal. Separate legal obligations and retention requirements need their own analysis.
lessons.example: A lecturer asks students to participate in research during a compulsory course. Participation is described as optional, but the lecturer also grades the students and no equivalent alternative exists. Compare an independent recruitment process with an equally accessible alternative and no academic consequences.
lessons.nuance: Consent to participate in a research study is an ethical decision and may coexist with a non-consent GDPR basis. Explain the distinction clearly so participants understand what withdrawal means in the actual study.

questions.statement: A preselected checkbox is sufficient affirmative GDPR consent.
questions.explanation: Consent requires a clear affirmative act; preselected boxes do not meet that standard.

questions.statement: Withdrawal of valid consent does not retrospectively invalidate earlier lawful consent-based processing.
questions.explanation: Article 7(3) expressly provides this.

questions.statement: The university must be able to demonstrate consent when relying on it.
questions.explanation: Article 7(1) places that responsibility on the controller.

questions.statement: A student signature proves freedom of choice regardless of the grading relationship.
questions.explanation: The actual conditions and possible detriment determine whether consent is free.

questions.statement: Consent to one optional promotional use need not cover unrelated marketing purposes.
questions.explanation: Specificity requires appropriate distinction between purposes.

questions.statement: A signed ethical participation form automatically establishes Article 9 explicit consent for every use.
questions.explanation: Ethical permission and explicit GDPR consent have different requirements and scope.

lessons.title: Public task in Dutch universities
lessons.objective: Analyze Article 6(1)(e) and its legal foundation in the Dutch higher-education context.
concepts: **A statutory foundation.** A task in the public interest or exercise of official authority requires a basis in EU or member-state law. The legal foundation need not specify every individual processing operation, but the processing must be necessary for the task. Identify the relevant law and explain the connection.

**Dutch university context.** The WHW describes functions of higher-education institutions and examination responsibilities. For example, Article 1.3 concerns institutional functions and Articles 7.12–7.12b concern examination boards. These are starting points for legal analysis, not a blanket authorization for every proposed data use.

**Separate purpose and necessity.** Teaching, scientific research and public knowledge transfer may form part of a university's statutory mission, but an optional profiling tool or marketing campaign is not automatically necessary for that mission. Consider less intrusive alternatives and applicable sector rules.

**Rights still matter.** Article 21(1) provides a right to object to public-task processing on grounds relating to the individual's situation. The controller must assess the applicable grounds for continuing. Research has a distinct Article 21(6) rule.
lessons.example: An examination board needs a student's assessed results to determine eligibility for a degree. Compare that statutory function with continuous collection of behavioral analytics from the same student to optimize advertising for a summer school. The latter cannot borrow the board's legal reasoning merely because both activities occur at the university.
lessons.nuance: The university's status, exact processing purpose and national legal basis need examination. Do not presume that a particular Dutch institution is a public authority for every activity, or that public task covers all research automatically.

questions.statement: Article 6(1)(e) requires a legal foundation under Article 6(3).
questions.explanation: The public-task basis must be grounded in EU or member-state law.

questions.statement: A reference to a university's mission is sufficient without assessing the necessity of the actual processing.
questions.explanation: The processing must be necessary for the legally grounded task.

questions.statement: Article 21(1) can apply to processing under public task.
questions.explanation: It specifically includes Article 6(1)(e).

questions.statement: A statutory examination function automatically authorizes unrelated marketing use of student records.
questions.explanation: The new purpose must be evaluated separately.

questions.statement: The legal foundation for public task need not describe every individual technical operation.
questions.explanation: Recital 45 recognizes that one law may suffice for several processing operations.

questions.statement: Public-task processing is categorically exempt from Article 9.
questions.explanation: Special-category conditions remain applicable.

lessons.title: Legitimate interests and balancing
lessons.objective: Apply the three-part legitimate-interest test and understand the KNLTB judgment.
concepts: **Purpose test.** Identify a specific, real and lawful interest of the controller or a third party. An abstract wish for more information is insufficient. Commercial interests are not automatically excluded, but they must still satisfy the other conditions.

**Necessity test.** Ask whether processing is actually needed to achieve that interest and whether an equally effective, less intrusive method exists. If the interest can be met without using personal data, this basis may not support the proposed processing.

**Balancing test.** Consider the nature of the data, reasonable expectations, dependency, potential harm and safeguards. A legitimate interest does not prevail automatically. Record the reasoning and provide required information about the interest; the right to object also matters.

**Case law.** In C-621/22 (KNLTB), the Court held that a commercial interest can potentially qualify without being expressly prescribed by law. It did not approve all commercial disclosures: necessity and balancing remained essential. The case is particularly relevant in the Netherlands because it involved the AP.
lessons.example: A university alumni association considers sharing graduate contact details with a commercial partner. Compare an approach that gives alumni an optional opportunity to contact the partner themselves. Consider reasonable expectations, necessity, the type of data and whether the university or association is acting as a public authority in the relevant task.
lessons.nuance: Article 6(1)(f) does not apply to processing by public authorities in performing their tasks. Direct marketing objections under Article 21(2)–(3) have different consequences from general Article 21(1) objections.

questions.statement: An interest can be commercial and still potentially qualify as legitimate.
questions.explanation: KNLTB confirms commercial interests are not categorically excluded; other conditions remain.

questions.statement: The KNLTB judgment means every sale of contact details is lawful.
questions.explanation: The Court retained the necessity and balancing requirements; it did not approve all sales.

questions.statement: An equally effective less intrusive alternative matters to the necessity test.
questions.explanation: Necessity is not satisfied merely by a preference for a more intrusive method.

questions.statement: Reasonable expectations of individuals are irrelevant if the controller has a financial interest.
questions.explanation: Reasonable expectations are relevant to balancing.

questions.statement: A direct marketing objection requires processing for that marketing purpose to stop.
questions.explanation: Article 21(3) requires cessation for that purpose.

questions.statement: A public authority performing its tasks can use legitimate interests as an alternative to public task.
questions.explanation: Article 6(1) expressly excludes this basis in that context.

lessons.title: Special categories and Article 9
lessons.objective: Apply the two-layer lawfulness assessment and distinguish special-category data from other sensitive information.
concepts: **Two layers.** Establish an Article 6 basis and a relevant exception to the Article 9(1) prohibition. The categories include health, genetic data, certain biometric data, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religion, trade union membership and data about sex life or sexual orientation.

**Biometric distinction.** A normal photograph is not automatically special-category biometric data. Article 9 addresses biometric data processed for unique identification. Technical processing and intended purpose matter. A photograph might nevertheless reveal other special categories depending on its use.

**Choose the actual exception.** Article 9(2) includes explicit consent, specified employment or social protection conditions, vital interests, legal claims, substantial public interest, healthcare, public health and research subject to requirements. Research under Article 9(2)(j) needs a legal foundation and safeguards. UAVG Article 24 supplies a Dutch conditional research exception; it is not a blanket exemption.

**Other sensitive data.** Grades, financial information and disciplinary records can be highly sensitive without necessarily being Article 9 categories. Article 10 separately governs criminal conviction and offence data. Security, minimization and risk assessment apply to all personal data.
lessons.example: A university stores disability information to provide accommodations. The examination board needs to know which accommodation applies, but may not need the medical diagnosis. Compare that with a health research project analyzing diagnoses, where the information itself is scientifically necessary. The purpose, conditions, access and safeguards differ.
lessons.nuance: Information may reveal health or another protected category indirectly. Do not decide solely from a column name or whether the data were supplied by the individual. Examine the actual meaning and intended inference.

questions.statement: A medical diagnosis is health data even when it is stored with a study code.
questions.explanation: Coding does not remove Article 9 when the record remains personal data.

questions.statement: Every ordinary portrait photograph is automatically special-category biometric data.
questions.explanation: The special biometric category concerns unique identification through biometric processing.

questions.statement: A lawful Article 6 basis alone is sufficient for processing health data.
questions.explanation: An applicable Article 9 exception is also required.

questions.statement: A research exception under Article 9(2)(j) requires appropriate safeguards and a legal foundation.
questions.explanation: The provision expressly refers to law and Article 89(1).

questions.statement: Criminal conviction data are subject to a separate Article 10 regime.
questions.explanation: Article 10 applies separate conditions rather than listing them in Article 9.

questions.statement: A grade is always an Article 9 special-category datum because it is confidential.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality and statutory special categories are distinct.

lessons.title: Controllers, processors and joint control
lessons.objective: Classify parties by what they actually do.
concepts: A controller determines purposes and means of processing. A processor acts on behalf of a controller.
Joint controllers jointly determine purposes and means; Article 26 requires an arrangement reflecting their responsibilities.
Article 28 requires sufficient processor guarantees and a binding agreement containing the prescribed terms.
lessons.example: A university instructs a survey hosting company to store responses. The company may be a processor for that activity; a partner university defining a joint study may be a joint controller.
lessons.nuance: A contract label does not settle the classification. A provider may have different roles for different processing purposes.

questions.statement: Two universities can be joint controllers without having identical responsibilities.
questions.explanation: Article 26 calls for a transparent allocation of responsibilities, not identical roles.

questions.statement: A company is a processor for all activities whenever a contract calls it a processor.
questions.explanation: Actual purposes and means determine the role for each activity.

questions.statement: A controller must assess whether a processor provides sufficient guarantees.
questions.explanation: Article 28(1) places this requirement on the controller.

lessons.title: Rights, transparency and automated decisions
lessons.objective: Recognize rights and their limits.
concepts: Articles 13 and 14 govern information provision. Access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability and objection have distinct conditions.
Erasure is not unconditional; Article 17(3) contains exceptions including legal obligations and certain public-interest purposes.
Article 22 concerns decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or similarly significant effects, subject to exceptions and safeguards.
lessons.example: A student asks for access to their personal data in a learning platform. The university must evaluate the request under Article 15 and respect other persons’ rights.
lessons.nuance: A nominal human signature is not necessarily meaningful review. Examine actual decision-making, not only the workflow diagram.

questions.statement: A valid erasure request can be refused for records that must be retained under an applicable legal obligation.
questions.explanation: Article 17(3)(b) provides an exception where retention is necessary.

questions.statement: The right to data portability applies to every lawful basis.
questions.explanation: Article 20 applies to automated processing based on consent or contract, subject to its conditions.

questions.statement: Article 22 addresses only decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects and are based solely on automated processing.
questions.explanation: These are the central conditions in Article 22(1); other GDPR duties can still apply outside it.

lessons.title: Accountability, security and DPIAs
lessons.objective: Understand when safeguards and impact assessment are required.
concepts: Controllers must demonstrate compliance and implement appropriate technical and organizational measures.
A DPIA is required where processing is likely to result in high risk to individuals. It assesses necessity, proportionality, risks and measures before processing.
If high risk remains absent measures to mitigate it, Article 36 requires prior consultation with the supervisory authority.
lessons.example: A university proposes systematic monitoring of students. A DPIA may be required based on the nature, scope, context and purpose.
lessons.nuance: A DPIA is not merely a security review, and its completion does not by itself establish lawfulness.

questions.statement: A DPIA examines risks to individuals’ rights and freedoms, not only risks to the university.
questions.explanation: The focus is the impact on natural persons.

questions.statement: A DPIA is required for every new spreadsheet containing personal data.
questions.explanation: The trigger is likely high risk, not the mere existence of personal data.

questions.statement: An existing security certification removes the controller’s accountability obligations.
questions.explanation: Certification may help demonstrate compliance but does not remove responsibility.

lessons.title: Scope, roles and research exclusions
lessons.objective: Separate AI Act roles from GDPR roles.
concepts: The AI Act regulates AI systems and certain models. It defines providers and deployers by their activities, not by GDPR classifications.
A university using an AI system under its authority can be a deployer. A university developing and putting its own AI system into service may be a provider.

Article 2(6) excludes systems/models and outputs specifically developed and put into service solely for scientific research and development. Article 2(8) separately addresses pre-market research, testing and development; real-world testing is not covered by that exclusion.
lessons.example: A lab builds a research-only model; a faculty separately adopts a commercial tool for administrative tasks. The two uses need different scope assessments.
lessons.nuance: An AI Act research exclusion does not exempt personal-data processing from GDPR. Reassess when intended purpose changes.

questions.statement: An AI Act deployer is necessarily a GDPR processor.
questions.explanation: These are separate legal classifications based on different activities.

questions.statement: A university’s internal use of a commercial AI system can fall within the AI Act.
questions.explanation: Organizational use under its authority can make it a deployer.

questions.statement: The AI Act scientific-research exclusion also removes GDPR obligations.
questions.explanation: GDPR remains separately applicable to personal-data processing.

lessons.title: AI literacy and prohibited practices
lessons.objective: Understand already applicable duties and prohibitions.
concepts: Amended Article 4 requires providers and deployers to support AI literacy of staff and others operating or using AI on their behalf. Measures should reflect knowledge, context and affected persons.
The July 2026 amendment removed the original wording requiring a sufficient level; the obligation to take literacy measures remains.
Article 5 prohibits specified practices, including emotion inference in workplaces and educational institutions based on biometric data, subject to the medical or safety exception.
lessons.example: A faculty organizes context-specific training for staff using generative AI and prohibits an emotion-recognition system intended to infer students’ emotions during examinations.
lessons.nuance: Article 4 does not mandate one standard training course or certificate. High-risk systems can entail additional obligations.

questions.statement: The 2026 amendment removed every obligation for deployers to support AI literacy.
questions.explanation: The amended Article 4 retains the duty to take measures to support literacy.

questions.statement: AI literacy measures should reflect how AI is used and who is affected.
questions.explanation: The amended text expressly includes context and affected people.

questions.statement: A university may infer student emotions from biometric data for ordinary classroom engagement monitoring without considering Article 5.
questions.explanation: The educational emotion-inference prohibition is directly relevant; ordinary engagement is not the medical/safety exception.

lessons.title: High-risk AI and the implementation calendar
lessons.objective: Recognize intended-purpose classification and distinguish future rules from current duties.
concepts: Annex III lists education and employment use cases. Article 6 governs classification, including a limited exception for systems that do not pose a significant risk, subject to conditions; profiling of natural persons defeats that exception.
High-risk requirements include risk management, data governance and human oversight. Provider and deployer duties differ.

The 2026 Digital Omnibus postpones Annex III high-risk rules to 2 December 2027 and relevant Annex I product rules to 2 August 2028. The general application date was 2 August 2026; prohibitions and literacy started in February 2025. Transitional rules matter.
lessons.example: A university considers AI for admissions ranking. It should plan for the high-risk framework, while applying GDPR and any AI Act obligations already in force.
lessons.nuance: High-risk does not mean prohibited. Classification depends on intended purpose and the applicable legal conditions. Dates should be rechecked before practical reliance.

questions.statement: Every AI tool used at a university is high-risk solely because its user is a university.
questions.explanation: The specific intended purpose and Article 6 classification criteria matter.

questions.statement: An Annex III admissions system can be high-risk even though its vendor is not a university.
questions.explanation: The intended admissions use, not the vendor’s institutional identity, drives classification.

questions.statement: The general Annex III high-risk application date is 2 December 2027 under the July 2026 amendments.
questions.explanation: The amendment extends this deadline; other duties may already apply.

lessons.title: Participation consent and research lawful bases
lessons.objective: Separate informed consent from the GDPR basis.
concepts: Agreement to participate in research and GDPR consent serve different purposes. A study can rely on another valid Article 6 basis while obtaining ethical participation consent.
GDPR consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent.
For special categories, an Article 9 condition is also necessary. Dutch UAVG Article 24 provides a conditional research exception.
lessons.example: A cognitive science study uses informed participation consent, while the university evaluates whether public task is the appropriate GDPR basis.
lessons.nuance: Recital 33 recognizes that some scientific research purposes cannot be fully identified initially, but it does not authorize unlimited consent.

questions.statement: A signed research participation form establishes GDPR consent for every later use of the data.
questions.explanation: GDPR consent has its own conditions and scope. Later purposes require separate consideration.

questions.statement: Ethical participation consent can coexist with a different GDPR lawful basis.
questions.explanation: The two concepts are distinct; the chosen GDPR basis must satisfy Article 6.

questions.statement: Scientific research automatically permits processing special-category data under Dutch law.
questions.explanation: Article 9 and UAVG Article 24 impose conditions; research status alone is not enough.

lessons.title: Secondary use, retention and research safeguards
lessons.objective: Understand compatibility and research-specific safeguards.
concepts: Further processing for scientific research is not considered incompatible with the initial purposes under Article 5(1)(b) when Article 89(1) applies.
Longer storage for research can be permitted subject to appropriate safeguards; GDPR itself sets no universal ten-year research retention period.
Article 89 requires safeguards, especially minimization. UAVG Article 44 allows certain rights to be limited in specified research/statistical circumstances.
lessons.example: A lab wishes to reuse interview records from an earlier project. It checks purpose, lawful basis, transparency, identifiability and safeguards before reuse.
lessons.nuance: Open science does not require public release of personal data. Institutional retention rules and funder requirements must be considered separately.

questions.statement: GDPR itself imposes a ten-year minimum retention period on all university research data.
questions.explanation: Retention depends on purpose, applicable law and safeguards; institutional requirements are separate.

questions.statement: Research compatibility under Article 5(1)(b) is linked to Article 89(1) safeguards.
questions.explanation: The special compatibility rule expressly refers to Article 89(1).

questions.statement: UAVG Article 44 removes all data subject rights for any research activity.
questions.explanation: It addresses specific rights and conditions, not a blanket exemption.

lessons.title: International collaborations and AI development
lessons.objective: Distinguish sharing arrangements, transfers and research exclusions.
concepts: Partners’ controller/processor roles depend on actual purposes and means. Sharing personal data must have a lawful basis and appropriate safeguards.
Chapter V applies to qualifying transfers to third countries or international organizations. Adequacy, appropriate safeguards or narrowly applicable derogations are different routes.
Research-only AI exclusions are purpose-dependent. A research system later deployed in student services must be reassessed.
lessons.example: A Dutch lab gives an external Canadian research partner access to identifiable study data. It checks the recipient and whether an adequacy decision covers that recipient, or another valid transfer route is needed.
lessons.nuance: Access from abroad may be relevant even without downloading. A collaboration agreement alone is not a Chapter V transfer mechanism.

questions.statement: A collaboration agreement alone establishes a valid GDPR transfer mechanism for all third-country recipients.
questions.explanation: Chapter V requires an applicable mechanism and conditions; an ordinary collaboration agreement is not sufficient.

questions.statement: A research-only AI system later used operationally should be reassessed under the AI Act.
questions.explanation: The scope exclusion depends on the system’s scientific-only purpose and use.

questions.statement: Adequacy decisions must be checked for their scope, rather than assuming they cover every recipient in a country.
questions.explanation: Adequacy can apply to a country, territory, specified sector or international organization.

lessons.title: Student records, examinations and retention
lessons.objective: Connect GDPR principles with Dutch education responsibilities.
concepts: Student administration and examination processing require a specific purpose, lawful basis, access controls and defined retention.
WHW Articles 7.12 and 7.12b establish the examination board and its responsibilities. This does not grant unrestricted access to every student record.
Erasure requests must be assessed against relevant legal obligations and other exceptions, rather than handled automatically.
lessons.example: A student requests deletion of assessment records during an appeal. The university considers applicable retention rules, examination responsibilities and the need to preserve evidence.
lessons.nuance: Retention periods for exam scripts may depend on institutional schedules and other rules. Do not infer a single period from GDPR or WHW.

questions.statement: The examination board’s statutory duties permit it to see every student’s health information without a necessity assessment.
questions.explanation: Access must still be justified and minimized; health data have extra protection.

questions.statement: A student’s erasure request can be limited by an applicable statutory retention obligation.
questions.explanation: Article 17(3)(b) may apply where processing is necessary to comply with a legal obligation.

questions.statement: The examination board has a statutory role in determining whether degree requirements are met.
questions.explanation: This follows from WHW Article 7.12(2).

lessons.title: Learning analytics, proctoring and accommodations
lessons.objective: Assess monitoring and sensitive student data.
concepts: Learning analytics and remote proctoring can involve profiling or systematic monitoring. A DPIA may be required where high risk is likely.
Information about disability or health is special-category data. An applicable Article 9 condition is required; access must be minimized.
AI intended to detect prohibited behavior during tests is listed in Annex III(3)(d); Article 6 classification and the updated implementation calendar matter.
lessons.example: A faculty compares invasive webcam monitoring with less intrusive assessment methods and considers the impact on students with disabilities.
lessons.nuance: Consent may be difficult to establish as freely given when students lack a genuine choice. Assess alternatives rather than assuming consent resolves monitoring risks.

questions.statement: Student disability information can constitute special-category health data.
questions.explanation: Information revealing physical or mental health is covered by Article 9.

questions.statement: A mandatory proctoring checkbox necessarily establishes freely given GDPR consent.
questions.explanation: A lack of real choice can undermine consent.

questions.statement: AI intended to monitor prohibited behavior during examinations is explicitly listed in Annex III.
questions.explanation: Annex III(3)(d) lists this use; Article 6 and transition dates still matter.

lessons.title: AI-assisted admissions and grading
lessons.objective: Distinguish high-risk AI classification, human review and automated decisions.
concepts: AI intended to determine access/admission or evaluate learning outcomes can be listed high-risk under Annex III(3), subject to Article 6.
GDPR Article 22 applies to solely automated significant decisions, with specific exceptions and safeguards. A human rubber stamp may not amount to genuine human involvement.
AI Act human oversight and GDPR automated-decision rules are separate requirements. High-risk application deadlines do not postpone GDPR.
lessons.example: A course uses an AI-generated grading suggestion. A qualified examiner independently evaluates the work and can change the proposed result.
lessons.nuance: Human review can matter for Article 22 but does not automatically remove an AI system from Annex III classification.

questions.statement: Adding an examiner’s approval button automatically makes the decision non-automated under GDPR.
questions.explanation: Actual meaningful involvement matters, not a nominal approval step.

questions.statement: An AI system evaluating learning outcomes can fall within Annex III even when an examiner reviews its output.
questions.explanation: Human review does not itself settle Article 6 classification.

questions.statement: The delayed AI Act high-risk deadline suspends GDPR Article 22 for university grading.
questions.explanation: GDPR applies independently.

lessons.title: Procurement, cloud services and subprocessors
lessons.objective: Recognize controller duties and processor chains.
concepts: A processor contract must include Article 28 requirements, including instructions, confidentiality, security, assistance and return/deletion provisions.
A processor needs specific or general written authorization before engaging another processor. General authorization requires notice of intended changes and opportunity to object.
Where a supplier uses data for its own purposes, its role for that activity must be assessed separately.
lessons.example: A university procures cloud transcription software. It investigates whether recordings are used for vendor training, who has access and where processing takes place.
lessons.nuance: An EU server location is not proof that all processing, support or transfers stay within the EEA.

questions.statement: A processor can engage a subprocessor without any written authorization if it remains responsible for the service.
questions.explanation: Article 28(2) requires specific or general written authorization.

questions.statement: Under general authorization, intended subprocessor changes must be communicated so the controller can object.
questions.explanation: Article 28(2) explicitly requires this opportunity.

questions.statement: An EU hosting address establishes that every remote support activity remains in the EEA.
questions.explanation: Access arrangements and actual recipients must be checked separately.

lessons.title: Staff monitoring, recruitment and health data
lessons.objective: Apply GDPR and AI Act concepts to employment.
concepts: Employee data processing requires a lawful basis and proportionality. Employment power imbalance can undermine freely given consent.
Health and absence-related data may be special-category data; Dutch law contains limited exceptions. Do not infer unrestricted employer access.
AI for recruitment, selection or specified worker-management decisions is listed in Annex III(4); workplace emotion inference is generally prohibited subject to the medical/safety exception.
lessons.example: HR considers an AI tool to rank applicants and a dashboard to track employees’ behavior. Each purpose and technology requires its own legal assessment.
lessons.nuance: High-risk obligations apply according to the updated calendar, while prohibited practices and GDPR already apply.

questions.statement: An employment contract makes any form of employee monitoring necessary for contract performance.
questions.explanation: Necessity and proportionality must be established for the specific processing.

questions.statement: AI intended to rank job applicants can be listed high-risk under the AI Act.
questions.explanation: Recruitment and selection are included in Annex III(4)(a).

questions.statement: An employer’s legitimate interest alone is enough to process special-category health data.
questions.explanation: An applicable Article 9 condition is also required.

lessons.title: Breaches, responsibilities and oversight
lessons.objective: Distinguish institutional accountability from specialist duties.
concepts: A personal data breach can concern confidentiality, integrity or availability. Controllers document breaches and notify the authority unless risk to individuals is unlikely.
Where notification is required, the controller must notify without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after awareness. Processors notify controllers without undue delay.
The DPO advises and monitors independently. The controller remains accountable. A high-risk breach may also require communication to affected individuals.
lessons.example: An email with student records goes to the wrong recipient. The university assesses risk, documents the event and determines whether notification is required.
lessons.nuance: Not every security incident is a personal data breach, and not every breach requires notification. Internal reporting deadlines can be stricter.

questions.statement: A controller must document personal data breaches even when notification to the authority is not required.
questions.explanation: Article 33(5) requires documentation of breaches and relevant facts.

questions.statement: A processor has the same 72-hour statutory notification deadline to the authority as a controller.
questions.explanation: The processor must notify the controller without undue delay; the controller assesses authority notification.

questions.statement: Appointing a DPO transfers the controller’s responsibility for compliance to the DPO.
questions.explanation: The DPO advises and monitors; accountability remains with the controller.
